title: A Portrait for the Smile
premise: Orsen Vasquez takes a teaching job in a fog-bound coastal town where students vanish one desk at a time, and the school's records insist they never existed. At her late grandmother's house, old family photographs begin showing an empty chair that wasn't there before—and each time it appears, someone Orsen loves grows fainter, forgettable, halfway gone. The chair belongs to a thing her grandmother once bargained with: an inheritance of memory that feeds on the unremembered. To save her found family—a janitor who keeps the count, two students who remember too much—Orsen must make herself visible to it, offering her own memories as ransom, and in the end she trades every recollection of her grandmother to close the count forever, waking to strangers she'll have to love all over again.
about_author: J. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former night-shift school custodian from the Pacific Northwest who writes horror about institutions, grief, and the things that live in attendance records. Their short fiction has appeared in several small-press anthologies; this is their first novel.

chapters.title: Attendance
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. On her first day at Hollow Creek Elementary, Orsen counts twenty-nine desks but thirty names on the roster, and no one finds this strange. She learns the previous teacher 'resigned by absence.' Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked as professional calm.

chapters.title: The Empty Chair
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Sorting her grandmother's house, Orsen finds photo albums where an extra wooden chair sits in every family picture—older photos show it fainter, newer ones sharper. Her aunt Rosa insists there has always been a chair. Beat: creeping dread beneath domestic routine.

chapters.title: Thirty Names
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. A student named Milo corrects her roll call unprompted, adding a name no record contains: 'Edda.' That afternoon Edda's desk is simply gone. Beat: first proof the missing-class problem is real, and Orsen is the only one counting.

chapters.title: Doors and Lights
chapters.summary: POV Wendell, the aging janitor. Wendell reveals he keeps a ledger of doors—he counts them shut each night because 'the building likes to be whole.' He warns Orsen: whatever you notice, don't write it down twice. Beat: wary alliance between two people who pay attention.

chapters.title: What Rosa Forgot
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Aunt Rosa calls, mid-sentence forgetting her own daughter's name; in the newest photograph, Rosa's image has thinned to watercolor. The chair now sits closer to the family. Beat: grief sharpening into urgency—the photographs are eating people.

chapters.title: The Count
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. In the school basement archive, Orsen finds decades of class photos, each with one more blurred face, and a ledger in her grandmother's handwriting: dates, names, and the word 'paid' beside each. Beat: horrified inheritance—grandma knew.

chapters.title: Milo Remembers
chapters.summary: POV Milo. Milo tells Orsen he remembers his sister, whom no one else can, and that she faded after sitting for a portrait at grandma's house. His mother's albums show only him. Beat: found-family tenderness between teacher and student, both holding impossible memories.

chapters.title: Portrait Sitting
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Following the ledger, Orsen locates the photographer's abandoned studio; inside, portraits of townspeople hang with their eyes scratched out, and one frame waits, empty, labeled VASQUEZ. Beat: the trap has been waiting for her personally.

chapters.title: Rules of the House
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell shares what grandma told him years ago: the thing in the chair collects the unclaimed—people no one actively remembers. Keep them named, keep them seen, keep the lights on. Beat: exposition as intimacy; Wendell confesses he lost his wife to a lapse of attention.

chapters.title: Fainter
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Milo begins slipping—teachers mark him absent while he sits in class; his mother sets one plate at dinner. Orsen photographs him daily and makes the whole staff say his name aloud. Beat: desperate, loving resistance through ritual.

chapters.title: The Bargain, Annotated
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Grandma's letters reveal the original deal: long life for the town in exchange for a periodic 'seat at the table,' renewed each generation by a Vasquez. Orsen is the heir whether she signs or not. Beat: betrayal and inheritance entwined—love used as collateral.

chapters.title: Parent-Teacher Night
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. At the school event, parents mingle with figures whose faces won't hold; when Orsen counts heads, there are four extra. One of them wears her grandmother's cardigan. Beat: public dread, private heartbreak—the dead are being worn.

chapters.title: What the Chair Wants
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Dream sequence: Orsen sits in the chair inside the photographs and hears the collector explain—it doesn't steal people; it accepts those the world stops carrying. Memory is the only currency. Beat: understanding the rules well enough to fear breaking them.

chapters.title: Evacuation Plan
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. Wendell and Orsen plan to get everyone out ahead of the count: gather the fading, keep them named, drive past the town line where the photographs can't follow. But the ledger shows the count falls due in three days. Beat: hope with a deadline.

chapters.title: Rosa's Last Album
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Rosa, nearly transparent now, gives Orsen the final album and her blessing, remembering just enough to say goodbye. The chair in the newest photo stands empty, waiting. Beat: devastating farewell—grief as fuel.

chapters.title: The Long Roll Call
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Orsen gathers Milo, three other fading children, and Wendell, and leads them through the school at night, speaking every name like a litany while the corridors rearrange and doors multiply. Beat: terror and solidarity—the count trying to finish itself.

chapters.title: One Short
chapters.summary: POV Wendell. At the town line, Wendell's count comes up one short: himself. He stayed behind once too long; his name is already in the ledger. He closes the door behind them and turns back toward the school. Beat: sacrifice, quiet and enormous.

chapters.title: The Studio Revisited
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Unable to leave Wendell, Orsen returns alone to the studio, where the empty frame now bears her face. She offers the trade the collector actually wants: not lives, but the memories that anchor the Vasquez line. Beat: the climax's terrible choice made willingly.

chapters.title: Paid in Full
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Inside the portrait, Orsen surrenders every memory of her grandmother—childhood kitchen, lullabies, the smell of coffee—watching each burn away as the chair empties across every photograph in town. Beat: cathartic loss; love given up to save love.

chapters.title: After the Count
chapters.summary: POV Milo. Weeks later, the school is ordinary, full, and bright. Milo and the recovered children visit Orsen, who remembers them but not why she fought so hard for them—or who taught her to count. Beat: bittersweet new beginning; found family persists beyond memory.

chapters.title: What Orsen Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Among her grandmother's effects, Orsen finds one photo the trade missed: grandma laughing in the garden, no chair anywhere. She doesn't know the woman, but she frames it anyway. Beat: tender ambiguity—inheritance outlasting remembrance.

chapters.title: A Portrait for the Smile
chapters.summary: POV Orsen. Closing the house at last, Orsen counts the doors, leaves the lights on out of habit she can't explain, and smiles at the framed stranger. Somewhere, a ledger closes its cover. Beat: resolution with a held breath—peace, vigilantly kept.
